signal.title: BIST 100
signal.standing: The 100 largest and most traded companies on Borsa İstanbul, Türkiye's only stock exchange. It is priced in lira, so its level carries the country's inflation as much as its earnings: read the direction, not the number.

signal.title: Ibovespa
signal.standing: The Ibovespa is the benchmark index of B3, Brazil's stock exchange in São Paulo and Latin America's largest, tracking its most traded shares. Iron ore, oil and Brazilian interest rates drive it.

signal.title: CAC 40
signal.standing: The 40 largest companies listed on Euronext Paris, France's main stock market. Luxury goods and energy groups dominate it, which leaves the index unusually exposed to Chinese consumer demand.

signal.title: TA-125
signal.standing: The 125 largest companies by market value on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, Israel's only stock market. Banks, defence contractors and technology firms carry most of its weight, and it trades Sunday to Thursday.

signal.title: SMI
signal.standing: The Swiss Market Index: the 20 largest companies on the SIX Swiss Exchange in Zurich, Switzerland's main market. Nestlé, Roche and Novartis carry it, which makes it defensive when the world turns risk-off.

signal.title: OMXS30
signal.standing: The 30 most traded companies on Nasdaq Stockholm, Sweden's main stock market. It is heavy in Nordic industrials and telecoms, which makes it an early read on how much European companies plan to spend on capital goods.

signal.title: DAX
signal.standing: Frankfurt's benchmark index, tracking the 40 largest companies listed on the Deutsche Börse. Carmakers, chemicals and industrial engineering dominate it, and roughly three-quarters of their revenue is earned outside Germany.

signal.title: Hang Seng
signal.standing: The Hang Seng Index tracks the largest and most traded companies on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. It is where mainland Chinese companies meet foreign capital, and the clearest daily read on how investors view China.

signal.title: FTSE 100
signal.standing: The Financial Times Stock Exchange 100: the 100 largest companies on the London Stock Exchange by market value. Most of their revenue is earned abroad, so a falling pound tends to push the index up.

signal.title: S&P/TSX Composite
signal.standing: Canada's main equity benchmark, tracking the largest companies listed in Toronto by market value. Energy, mining and the big banks make up most of its weight, so it trades more like a commodity basket than a broad economy.

signal.title: S&P 500
signal.standing: A capitalisation-weighted index of 500 large companies listed on US exchanges, and the default benchmark for American equities. Trillions in pension and index funds track it, so most Western retirement savings move with it.

signal.title: S&P/ASX 200
signal.standing: The 200 largest companies listed on the Australian Securities Exchange in Sydney, weighted by market value. Miners and banks dominate it, and it is often the first major market to react to Chinese demand data.

signal.title: FTSE MIB
signal.standing: The 40 most traded companies on Borsa Italiana in Milan, Italy's main stock market. Banks and utilities dominate it, which makes it the equity market most sensitive to Italian sovereign debt spreads.

signal.title: SSE Composite
signal.standing: Mainland China's main board, in Shanghai, tracking every A- and B-share listed there — state banks, insurers and industrial groups by weight. Largely closed to foreign investors, so it follows domestic policy more than global risk appetite.

signal.title: IDX Composite
signal.standing: The IDX Composite tracks every company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in Jakarta. It is the market of the world's largest Muslim-majority country, heavily weighted to commodities and banking.

signal.title: MERVAL
signal.standing: The most traded shares on Bolsas y Mercados Argentinos, the Buenos Aires exchange and Argentina's main market. Priced in pesos, which have repeatedly lost most of their value, so it rises even in bad years.

signal.title: TAIEX
signal.standing: The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Stock Index, covering the listed common shares on the exchange in Taipei. TSMC alone is roughly a third of it, which makes this the most concentrated major market on the map.

signal.title: NASDAQ-100
signal.standing: The 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq stock market in the United States, weighted by market value. A handful of tech giants dominate it, so it trades as a bet on American technology and chips.

signal.title: SENSEX
signal.standing: The SENSEX, short for Sensitive Index, tracks 30 large, heavily traded companies on the Bombay Stock Exchange in Mumbai, India. The exchange is Asia's oldest, founded in 1875, and the index is the benchmark for Indian equities.

signal.title: Nikkei 225
signal.standing: The Nikkei 225 tracks 225 large companies listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, Japan's main market, and weights them by share price. Tokyo is Asia's largest exchange and the first major market to price each trading day.

signal.title: FTSE/JSE All Share
signal.standing: The FTSE/JSE All Share tracks nearly every company listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, South Africa's main market, weighted by size. It is Africa's largest exchange by far, and miners and a few global giants dominate it.

signal.title: FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI
signal.standing: The 30 largest companies by market value on Bursa Malaysia in Kuala Lumpur. The exchange is the world's largest market for Islamic finance instruments and the centre of the global sukuk trade.

signal.title: IBEX 35
signal.standing: The 35 most traded companies on the Bolsa de Madrid, Spain's main stock exchange. Its big banks earn heavily in Latin America, which makes the index a proxy for both regions.

validated.text: Brazilian stocks on São Paulo's B3 exchange gained 5.0% across four sessions in the final days before a national vote. The run-up has been turbulent: the final debate was cancelled two days before the vote, and the deposit insurer paid $7.7bn for Banco Master's collapse. Nothing in the coverage ties the rally to either event.

Israeli stocks had a soft week: the Tel Aviv market's main gauge gave up 3.5% over five sessions to 15 September, reversing its earlier direction. Its bank, defence and tech tilt means a few large names set the tone. The stretch coincided with Israeli shelling in south Lebanon and a US-approved bomb sale; coincidence is not cause.

Canadian stocks on the Toronto Stock Exchange fell 3.1% over 4 straight sessions from 2026-09-03 to 2026-09-10. The slide overlapped with a trade fight with the US: Washington banned Canadian dairy, alcohol and motorcycles outright, and Canada's $20 billion in counter-tariffs took effect Tuesday. No report here links the drop to either step.

Argentine stocks on the Buenos Aires exchange, Bolsas y Mercados Argentinos, fell 9.1% across 8 straight sessions to 2026-09-29. The slide came as poverty jumped 4.1 points to 32.3% in six months and Argentina gave Britain 2 weeks to halt a Falklands oil project, though neither report ties these to the market.

Stocks on the Taiwan Stock Exchange in Taipei rose 4.9% over 4 straight sessions, from 2026-09-15 to 2026-09-21. The only related coverage in that window was a 2026-09-16 story on Lithuania's lasers guarding Taiwan's chips. It is about chip-supply security, and nothing supplied connects it to the rise.

Big American tech stocks on the Nasdaq in the United States gained 5.3% over 5 sessions to 2026-09-23. News that week about the giants that dominate the index included Microsoft's plan for $10 billion-plus across 4 Gulf states by 2030 and Nvidia's AI push in the United Arab Emirates. None of that coverage links these stories to the rise.

South African stocks on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange fell 4.3% over 5 sessions to 2026-09-30. The slide ran alongside a rough stretch of news: US sanctions that Pretoria disputes, and a Durban terminal handling 30% less cargo after a software switch. The coverage does not tie these events to the fall.

Shares on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange fell 2.6% in one session to 2 October. The drop coincided with friction involving China: it demanded copper guarantees for the Anglo Teck merger, MI5 said 100+ UK academics joined Chinese-funded projects, and the Philippines said it forced a Chinese survey ship from Batanes. The coverage ties none to the fall.
